data.title: The Old Hungarians in written sources of the 9th century
data.excerpt: The image of the ancestors of today’s Hungarians in the chronicles of the time – written above all by Frankish chroniclers – is truly not a flattering one. Excerpts from Liudprand of Cremona, Regino of Prüm, the Annalista Saxo and Johannes Aventinus show what reputation these foreign nomads had in Europe from the time when they invaded the Carpathian Basin.
data.metaTitle: The Old Hungarians in written sources of the 9th century
data.metaDescription: The image of the Old Hungarians in the chronicles of their own time, from the years of their invasion of the Carpathian Basin, as Frankish writers saw them.

children.text: The image of the ancestors of today’s Hungarians in the chronicles of the 9th century, that is, of the times when they invaded the Carpathian Basin, as their contemporaries – above all the Frankish chroniclers – saw them, is truly not very flattering. I bring you excerpts from several interesting chronicles of this period which record what reputation these foreign nomads had in Europe.
I shall leave out, because you will find them elsewhere on this site.

(the 10th century) contains an interesting mention of how the Frankish king Arnulf brought it about that the Hungarians reached the territories of present-day Slovakia, and what strategic mistake he made when he had the abatis, or barriers, removed, which formed a natural wall against enemies from the east.

blocks.text: Meanwhile Arnulf, king of those peoples who dwell in the north, being unable to overcome Svatopluk, duke of the Moravians, of whom we made mention above and who manfully withstood him in battle, removed – alas – those strongly fortified obstacles of which we said before that they are commonly called barriers (abatis?), and called to his aid the people of the Hungarians, greedy, bold, not knowing almighty God, well versed in every crime and craving only for slaughter and plunder – if indeed that can be called aid which not long afterwards, when he had died, became a grave danger, nay even destruction, both to his own people and to the other peoples living to the south and the west. What then? Svatopluk is overcome, subdued, made tributary; but not he alone. O you blind desire of King Arnulf for power! O those unhappy and bitter days! The overthrow of a single man becomes the ruin of all Europe. Blind ambition, to how many wives do you bring widowhood, to fathers the death of their children, to maidens dishonour, to priests and to the people of God captivity, to churches abandonment and to inhabited lands desolation! But let us return to the matter. So, after the defeat of Svatopluk, duke of the Moravians, Arnulf ruled in the peace that followed. The Hungarians meanwhile, when they had observed the outcome and had surveyed the land, were devising evil in their hearts, which came to light later.

children.text: Also worthy of note is an excerpt from

, which records the mentions of the Old Hungarians in perhaps the greatest detail and to a large extent also factually and objectively. Regino was abbot in Prüm and later worked in Trier. He wrote several works. His chronicle brings less tendentious reports. He died in 915.

blocks.text:
In the year 889 from the incarnation of the Lord there came forth the people of the Hungarians, the fiercest and crueller than all monsters, in past centuries unknown for the reason that it was nowhere named, from somewhere in the Scythian kingdoms and marshes which the Don spreads out without end by its course.
From there, then, the said people was driven out of its own seats by the neighbouring peoples who are called the Pechenegs, for these outweighed them both in number and in valour, and their native land, as we have already said, did not suffice for dwelling because of the enormous growth of the population. And so, when they had been driven out by them by force, they take leave of their homeland and set out on a journey to seek new lands which they might inhabit and where they might build themselves seats.
First they wander through the wastes of the Pannonians and the Avars and seek their daily sustenance from hunting and fishing. Later they break with frequent hostile raids into the lands of the Carantanians, the Moravians and the Bulgarians; few men they kill with the sword, but many thousands with arrows, which they loose from bows made of horn with such skill that it is hard to avoid being hit by them.
blocks.author: Regino of Prüm

children.text: The work came into being in the middle of the 12th century and records data from the years 741 – 1139. The author drew on written sources hitherto unknown or already lost.

blocks.text:
890 [...] They (the Hungarians), however, do not know how to fight in formation or how to take cities. It would not be possible to resist them if they were as persevering as they are aggressive. They fight on horses galloping forward or fleeing back; often they feign an attack and cannot fight for long, at the height of the battle they leave the field and soon afterwards return to it from their flight, so that you are forced to fight the decisive battle at the moment when you already think you have won.
They do not feed like men, but like wild beasts, on raw meat and by drinking blood. The hearts of the men they have captured they divide into pieces and eat them as a medicine. They cannot be softened by any compassion. They shave their hair with a knife down to the skin; on horseback they are accustomed to move, to stand, to speak and to think. With great thoroughness they teach their children and their slaves to ride horses and to shoot from them.
Like the women, the men too are of a wanton, rebellious, treacherous and insolent nature. They are always restless, inclined to quarrels both abroad and at home; by nature they are taciturn, more ready for deeds than for words.
These laid waste the lands mentioned above, and the kingdom of Italy as well. Until Arnulf’s time they were separated off by the obstacles which people call barriers, and so had no possibility of setting out either to the west or to the south. After their removal Arnulf, with the help of the Hungarians, defeated Svatopluk and broke into the Moravian kingdom with an army, destroying everything he found outside the city. And when the fruit trees had been torn up by the roots, Svatopluk asked for peace and gave his son as a hostage, and later obtained it. Arnulf governed the empire in peace. The Hungarians, however, having observed the outcome and surveyed the lands, were devising evil in their hearts, which came to light later.
blocks.source: Annalista Saxo (the Saxon Annalist), the middle of the 12th century

blocks.text:
In that same year, which was the eight hundred and eighty-ninth of the Christian era, our neighbours the Hungarians, who in their own language call themselves Magyars... came, after crossing the Don, into Europe and into Sarmatian Germania. Some assert that they left their fathers’ seats for the sake of better soil, others that it was in order to relieve the all too great number of kings at home, others that they were driven out by their neighbours, while a part again asserts that they were invited by Arnulf against the Slavs and Svatopluk, whose empire was at that time the most extensive in lower Germania, and that they were let into Germania by him.
But I shall return to the Hungarians: they, wandering for three years through the territory of the eastern part of great Germania and through the territories of both Sarmatias, passed through very savage peoples across extensive wastes and plains, seeking their sustenance by pillage, plunder and hunting. Only in the fourth year do they obtain permanent seats from Arnulf. Then they fall upon Dacia – which stretches, together with the Danube, towards the east – beyond the river Tisza. They slaughter and destroy the Avars and the Huns (of whom we said that they had been pushed out and driven from Noricum and from the Pannonias by Pippin and the Bavarians) and occupy their land, and hold it to this day. Then they took over in Europe the nation and the name of the Avars and the Huns as their own. They dwelt here by the Danube and lived partly in Dacia, partly in the Pannonias and in Noricum, for five hundred and nine years up to that time.
Then these Hungarians afflict the Venedi with destruction rather than with defeat, those who inhabited Dacia and were obedient to Svatopluk, the Moravian king. They subdue the whole of Dacia and here to this day they are called "the Hungarians in Great Germania". After the death of Arnulf and the killing of the Moravian kings Mojmír and Svatopluk they occupy part of Moravia and, crossing the Danube, fall upon Bavaria. From the kingdom of the Bavarians they tear away Pannonia lying by the Danube: they drink human blood, but such things it will be fitting to set out only in their proper places. Now I shall return to the sequence of events. (...)
blocks.author: Johannes Aventinus
